explanations.explanation: Amos says it himself: “this lamentation I take up against you.” A lamentation is a song of mourning, so he isn't coming with a pep talk. He's grieving out loud over the house of Israel. You don't clap along to this one.

A battle cry makes sense when the news is heavy, I get it. But Amos calls what he takes up “this lamentation,” and that's a mourning song. Nobody is charging anywhere in this verse. He's grieving, friend.

I'd love for this to open with a victory song, believe me. But Amos says he takes up “this lamentation” against the house of Israel, which is a song of mourning. That's about as far from a party tune as you can get. This message starts sad.

Amos says, “She lies abandoned on her land, with no one to raise her up.” Picture reaching for a hand and finding empty air. That's the whole scene, and it's a heavy one. I think that's why he sings it as a lament.
It's kind of you to send her sons running over, and I like the heart behind it. But the verse says she lies abandoned “with no one to raise her up.” Sons never show up in it. Nobody does.
A king rushing in to lift her would be a nice twist, friend. The verse doesn't give us one, though. It says she lies abandoned on her land “with no one to raise her up.” No king, no helper, no one.

The LORD says, “The city that marches out a thousand strong will have but a hundred left.” That's one out of every ten still standing. It's a hard number to hear. Those little words “but a” carry a lot.
Five hundred would be half, and half would already hurt. But the verse is tougher than that. It says the city “will have but a hundred left.” That's a tenth of a thousand.
Nine hundred sounds like a city that came through okay, and I wish it did. The words are “will have but a hundred left.” You flipped the numbers, friend. It's a hundred that remain, not nine hundred.

The LORD says, “the one that marches out a hundred strong will have but ten left in the house of Israel.” Smaller city, smaller number, same shape. Both lose nine out of every ten. The pattern is stacked on purpose, and you spotted it.

I can see why you'd hesitate, but the text says it plainly. The city that marches out a hundred strong “will have but ten left in the house of Israel.” That matches the first line, where a thousand shrinks down to a hundred. Ten it is.
“Seek Me and live!” That's what the LORD says to the house of Israel. After all that mourning, He opens a door. Notice it's an invitation, not another threat.

With all the marching and losses in verse 3, war feels like the next move. But what the LORD says in verse 4 is, “Seek Me and live!” That's an invitation, not orders to suit up. He's calling them toward Himself.

Building more altars sounds busy and religious, and you can see why you'd pick it. But the LORD says, “Seek Me and live!” In the very next verse He points them away from Bethel and Gilgal. The call is to seek Him, not to build something.

explanations.answer: Gilgal will go into exile and Bethel will come to nothing
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “…Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will come to nothing.” Those are the very places people were heading toward. So heading there is a dead end. He wants them to seek Him instead.

explanations.answer: Gilgal will be rebuilt and Bethel will grow strong
explanations.explanation: That's a cheerful forecast, and I'd sign up for it. But the LORD says the opposite: “…Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will come to nothing.” Nothing there gets built up. Only seeking Him leads to life.

explanations.answer: Gilgal will be spared and Bethel will become a fortress
explanations.explanation: A fortress would be quite the upgrade, friend. But the text says “…Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will come to nothing.” No sparing, no walls. Both places are on their way out.

The LORD says, “…He will sweep like fire through the house of Joseph.” If you've ever left a tray in the oven too long, you know how fast things go. This fire is far bigger than that. Seeking Him is the way to live.

A flood is a good guess, since verse 8 does talk about the sea's waters being poured out. But here, in verse 6, He says He will “sweep like fire through the house of Joseph.” The picture is fire. Fire it is.
A storm is a fair guess for something that sweeps through. But the word in verse 6 is “fire.” He says He will sweep like fire through the house of Joseph. No thunder in this one, just flames.

I understand hoping somebody grabs a bucket. But the text says the fire “will devour everything, with no one at Bethel to extinguish it.” So nobody there puts it out. That's why the call to seek the LORD comes first.

False it is. The fire “will devour everything, with no one at Bethel to extinguish it.” The people had been going to Bethel, and there's no firefighter waiting there. The only safe move is to seek the LORD.

It's all one sentence about one Person. “He who made the Pleiades and Orion” also “summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth,” and the verse ends, “the LORD is His name.” Star groups overhead, the sea below, and He handles both. That's who Amos says is speaking.

It might feel like too much for one Person, but the verse ties it together. He who made the Pleiades and Orion is also the One who “summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth.” Then it says, “the LORD is His name.” It's all the same LORD.
The verse says, “He flashes destruction on the strong, so that fury comes upon the stronghold.” A stronghold is a place built to be safe. Walls don't stop Him here. You got it, friend.

A stronghold feels like it should be the safe spot, I get that. But the verse says, “He flashes destruction on the strong, so that fury comes upon the stronghold.” The place built for safety doesn't escape. So it's true.

explanations.answer: They will never live in them
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “…you will never live in the stone houses you have built.” The reason in the text is that they trample on the poor and exact a tax of grain from him. They did all that building and don't get to move in. Think of paying for the whole house and never getting a key.

Stone does sound like it lasts, and that's probably what pulled you. But the LORD says, “…you will never live in the stone houses you have built.” The houses aren't the promise here. Living in them is what gets taken away.

explanations.answer: They will go to the poor
explanations.explanation: I like that ending, friend. But the verse never says who ends up with the houses. What it says is, “…you will never live in the stone houses you have built.” Only the builders' loss is stated.

I get why you'd think a vineyard comes with a reward. But the LORD says, “you will never drink the wine from the lush vineyards you have planted.” They did the planting and get no sip. So the answer is false.
False is right. The LORD says, “you will never drink the wine from the lush vineyards you have planted.” Same pattern as the stone houses. They put in all that work and don't get to enjoy the wine.
The LORD says, “You oppress the righteous by taking bribes.” A bribe is a payment to tilt a decision. It goes straight against the integrity verse 10 mentions. You nailed it.
Stolen flocks would be a serious thing, but this verse doesn't mention flocks. It says, “You oppress the righteous by taking bribes.” That's the how. Stay with what's written.

Boundary stones are a fair thing to think of, but they don't show up here. The LORD says, “You oppress the righteous by taking bribes.” Bribes are the answer in this verse. Nobody is touching any stones.
I'd love a fair hearing at the gate to be the picture, friend. But the LORD says, “you deprive the poor of justice in the gate.” So they don't get one. That's why the answer is false.

False, and the text is clear. The LORD says, “you deprive the poor of justice in the gate.” The place where they should find justice is the place they're shut out. Later He tells them to “establish justice in the gate” (Amos 5:15).

Verse 13 says, “Therefore, the prudent keep silent in such times, for the days are evil.” So the prudent stay quiet. Sometimes silence is the loudest sign of how heavy the times are. You read that right.

It might sound like the prudent would speak up, and I like that instinct. But the verse says, “Therefore, the prudent keep silent in such times, for the days are evil.” So they stay quiet. True is the answer.

The LORD says, “…the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be with you, as you have claimed.” After all those warnings, here is a promise to be with them. That's the best thing on the whole table. Seek good and you live.
A king sounds like a big reward, but no king is promised here. The LORD says, “…the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be with you, as you have claimed.” His presence is the promise. Not a throne.

Double the harvest would be a nice bonus, no doubt. But the verse promises something else: “…the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be with you, as you have claimed.” Nothing about harvest here. He promises to be with them.

The LORD says, “Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the gate.” Back in verse 7 there were those who turned justice into wormwood, so this is the reverse. The gate is where the poor were being denied it. Now He tells them to put it back.
Peace is a lovely word, and I can see why you reached for it. But the verse says, “Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the gate.” Justice is the word. Peace isn't in the verse.
Worship feels like a natural thing to finish with, friend. But the verse says, “Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the gate.” The gate is where justice goes. Worship isn't named there.
The verse says, “Perhaps the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.” A remnant is what's left. It's a small word with a lot of hope in it. You got it.

I see where the thought comes from, but kings of Judah aren't in this verse. It says, “Perhaps the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.” A remnant is what's left of the house of Joseph. That's who the perhaps is for.

Edom, a nation, doesn't appear in this verse. It says, “Perhaps the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.” The remnant of Joseph is what's left of Israel. That's where the hope lands.
The verse says, “The farmer will be summoned to mourn, and the mourners to wail.” Even the one working the field gets called in. Nobody gets to skip it. The grief spreads wide.

A farmer feels like someone busy enough to be left out, but the text includes him. “The farmer will be summoned to mourn, and the mourners to wail.” So true is the answer. The wailing reaches out into the fields.

explanations.answer: He will pass through their midst
explanations.explanation: The LORD says, “There will be wailing in all the vineyards, for I will pass through your midst,” says the LORD. That's the reason, right in His own words. It's a sobering line. You read it well.

explanations.answer: He will hide His face from them
explanations.explanation: Hiding His face is a strong picture, but it isn't in this verse. The LORD gives His reason Himself: “There will be wailing in all the vineyards, for I will pass through your midst,” says the LORD. He says He will pass through. That's the reason given.

explanations.answer: He will send a famine on them
explanations.explanation: With vineyards in view, famine is an easy guess. But the verse never mentions one. It says, “There will be wailing in all the vineyards, for I will pass through your midst,” says the LORD. The reason is that He passes through.
